Abated
ə-bāt'əd
v. (diminished, lessened; used of floodwaters, of a valuation, of anger, and of a man's natural force)
Old French abatre, to beat down, from Latin ad and battere, to beat. The English keeps the sense of something brought down from a height — water, price, or wrath.

Biblical Definition

Four uses, and each one instructive. The flood: “Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground” (Gen 8:8) — and the reason they abated is given a few verses earlier: “God remembered Noah… and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged” (Gen 8:1). The law: a field sanctified after the jubile is reckoned by the years remaining, “and it shall be abated from thy estimation” (Lev 27:18) — the price falls because the time does, which is honest accounting written into the worship of God. Anger: Gideon turns away the wrath of Ephraim with a soft answer, and “their anger was abated toward him, when he had said that” (Jdg 8:3). And a man: “And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated” (Deu 34:7). That last is the exception that proves the rule, for natural force is exactly what does abate in every other man; Moses is buried by God with his strength unspent.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to abate as to beat down, to pull down, to destroy; to lessen, to diminish, to moderate; and in law, to deduct from a sum or a valuation.

expand to see more

ABATE, v.t. [Fr. abattre, to beat down.] To beat down; to pull down; to destroy in any manner.

2. To lessen; to diminish; to moderate. Abate your speed.

3. To deduct; as, to abate a sum from an account.

ABATE, v.i. To decrease, or become less in strength or violence. The waters were abated. Gen. viii.

Key Scripture

Gen 8:8 — "Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground;"

Gen 8:1 — "And God remembered Noah, and every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark: and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged;"

Deu 34:7 — "And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated."

Lev 27:18 — "But if he sanctify his field after the jubile, then the priest shall reckon unto him the money according to the years that remain, even unto the year of the jubile, and it shall be abated from thy estimation."

Modern Corruption

Floods are said to recede and tempers to cool as though by their own nature, while Genesis 8:1 assigns the abating to God remembering a man in a boat.

expand to see more

The waters did not simply drain away. Scripture puts a cause in front of the effect, and the cause is a Person: God remembered Noah, and made a wind to pass over the earth. That is the difference between the biblical account of the world and every account in which processes run themselves and God is at most the one who started them. A Christian may study evaporation and hydrology with the greatest diligence — the study is a good work and the regularity it describes is God's faithfulness — but he does not conclude from a mechanism that no one is governing it. Noah, for his part, is not idle either. He sends the dove, and sends her again, and waits seven days between; faith in the God who remembers is not the enemy of patient observation, it is what makes it bearable.

The Levitical use is the plainest place in Scripture where a valuation is honestly reduced. If a man sanctified his field after the jubile, the priest reckoned the years remaining and abated the estimate accordingly; the sanctuary did not take advantage of a worshipper's zeal to charge him for years that no longer existed. That is a small verse with a long reach, because religious institutions have a standing temptation to accept whatever a devout man will pay. And Deuteronomy 34:7 gives the other end of the word. Every man's natural force abates; the wonder recorded of Moses is that his did not, and the record is set down at the moment of his death, on the mountain, alone with God. He did not fail; he was taken. Which is the answer Scripture gives to men who dread the abating of their own strength: the strength is not the point of the life, and its keeping is not in the man.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chaser (H2637), to lack or decrease, of the flood waters; garar and garaa (H1639), to diminish, of the abated estimation; raphah (H7503), to slacken, of anger.

expand to see more

Hebrew chaser (H2637) — to diminish, to be lacking; the waters were abated from off the face of the ground; Genesis 8:8.

Hebrew shakak (H7918) — to subside, to assuage; the waters asswaged when God made a wind to pass; Genesis 8:1.

Hebrew gara (H1639) — to diminish, to take away; abated from thy estimation; Leviticus 27:18.

Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to slacken; their anger was abated toward him; Judges 8:3.

Hebrew leach (H3893) — freshness, natural force; not abated in Moses at a hundred and twenty; Deuteronomy 34:7.

Usage

"“To see if the waters were abated” — and God had remembered Noah first."

"“It shall be abated from thy estimation” — honest accounting written into the worship of God."

"“Nor his natural force abated” — the exception, recorded at a grave God dug."
